name: Teotihuacán
region: State of Mexico, 50 km north-east of Mexico City
tagline: The City of the Gods: a vast grid of pyramids, temples and avenues, built two thousand years ago by a civilisation whose name we do not know, centred on the Pyramid of the Sun.
highlight: Climbing the Pyramid of the Sun or walking the Avenue of the Dead at opening, when the site is quiet and the light is low.
shortDescription: One of the largest cities of the ancient Americas, with the third-largest pyramid in the world, murals, a citadel and a two-kilometre ceremonial avenue, an hour from Mexico City.
metaDescription: A Teotihuacán travel guide: the Pyramid of the Sun and Moon, the Avenue of the Dead, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, murals, how to get there from Mexico City and a half-day plan.
suggestedStay: Half a day to a day
nearestAirport: Mexico City Benito Juárez (MEX), about 1 hour 15 minutes
knownFor: The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the Avenue of the Dead, the murals
goodFor: Archaeology, walking, history, a day from Mexico City

intro: Teotihuacán was, at its height around 450 CE, one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 or more inhabitants. It was laid out on a grid, with a ceremonial avenue, the Avenue of the Dead, running for about 2 km between monumental pyramids and palaces. Its people are known as the Teotihuacanos, but we do not know what they called themselves or what language they spoke.

The Aztecs found the city in ruins in the 14th century, and, awed, named it Teotihuacán, 'the place where the gods were created', and they believed the gods had sacrificed themselves there to create the sun. The names of its buildings, such as the Pyramid of the Sun and the Avenue of the Dead, are Aztec inventions.

The site, about 50 km north-east of Mexico City, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1987. Its central monuments are the Pyramid of the Sun, about 65 metres high, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Citadel, with the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, and many of its apartment compounds still hold painted murals. It is a big, hot, open site, and its scale is best absorbed early in the morning.

whyVisit.intro: Teotihuacán is the most impressive pre-Hispanic site near Mexico City, and one of the great cities of the ancient world.

points.title: The Pyramid of the Sun
points.text: About 65 metres high and 220 metres on each side, it is one of the largest pyramids in the world, and visitors can climb its 248 steps.

points.title: The Avenue of the Dead
points.text: A grand 2 km avenue lined with platforms and temples, which gives a sense of the city's scale and planning.

points.title: The Temple of the Feathered Serpent
points.text: A pyramid covered in carved serpent heads and stylised feathers, in the Citadel.

points.title: Murals
points.text: Painted murals in the residential compounds and the site museum show gods, animals and ritual scenes in bright colours.

points.title: An hour from the capital
points.text: It is easy to visit in half a day, and it combines well with a lunch in a nearby cave restaurant.

attractionsIntro: The site is large and mostly exposed. Allow three to four hours.

attractions.name: The Pyramid of the Sun
attractions.text: The largest structure in Teotihuacán, built around 100 CE, with a steep stair to the top and views over the whole city.
attractions.tip: Climb early. Rules change, so check whether climbing is allowed.

attractions.name: The Pyramid of the Moon
attractions.text: A smaller pyramid at the northern end of the Avenue of the Dead, with a plaza in front. Its view down the avenue is the best in the site.

attractions.name: The Avenue of the Dead

image.file: File:Avenue of the Dead at Teotihuacan2.jpg
image.alt: The long Avenue of the Dead at Teotihuacán with the Pyramid of the Sun beyond

attractions.text: The ceremonial spine of the city, about 2 km long, lined with the remains of temples and palaces. Walking it takes about 40 minutes.
attractions.tip: Walk from the south entrance to the Pyramid of the Moon.

attractions.name: The Ciudadela and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent
attractions.text: A vast sunken enclosure with the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, decorated with carved serpent heads and thought to have been the centre of political power.

attractions.name: The Palace of Quetzalpapalotl
attractions.text: A residential compound with carved columns and painted murals of butterflies and birds.
attractions.tip: Near the Pyramid of the Moon.

attractions.name: The site museum
attractions.text: A well-designed museum with finds, models and murals, which helps you make sense of the site.

thingsToDoIntro: A visit to Teotihuacán is best planned around the heat and the crowds.

thingsToDo.title: Arrive at opening
thingsToDo.text: The gates open at about 09:00, and the site is cool, quiet and photogenic for the first hour.
thingsToDo.tip: Take the first bus from Mexico City.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the avenue
thingsToDo.text: Start at the Pyramid of the Moon and walk south, stopping at the palaces and the Citadel.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring a hat, water and sunscreen.

thingsToDo.title: Hire a guide
thingsToDo.text: A licensed guide explains the symbolism and history, which is hard to grasp alone.

thingsToDo.title: Have lunch in a cave restaurant
thingsToDo.text: La Gruta, a restaurant in a natural cave near the site, serves Mexican food in an atmospheric setting.

thingsToDo.title: Take a balloon flight
thingsToDo.text: Sunrise hot-air balloon flights float over the pyramids.

thingsToDo.title: Try obsidian and craft shops
thingsToDo.text: Obsidian carvers sell tools and jewellery near the site.

foodIntro: Eating options near the site are limited, but the area is known for barbacoa and pulque.

foods.name: Barbacoa
foods.text: Lamb slow-cooked in an underground pit and served in tacos or by the kilo.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants and stalls near the site.

foods.name: Pulque
foods.text: A slightly fermented agave drink, sweet and sour, traditional in this region.

foods.name: Tlacoyos and quesadillas
foods.text: Masa cakes and folded tortillas with fillings.

foods.name: Nopales and mole
foods.text: Cactus paddles and sauces, prepared traditionally.

foods.name: Fresh fruit and juices
foods.text: Prickly pear (tuna) and other fruit sold by vendors.

accommodation.intro: Most visitors go as a day trip from Mexico City, but a few hotels and guesthouses near the site allow an early start.

areas.name: San Juan Teotihuacán
areas.text: Simple hotels and guesthouses within a few kilometres of the site.

areas.name: Mexico City
areas.text: A much wider range, an hour away.

gettingThere.intro: Teotihuacán is about 50 km north-east of Mexico City.

options.text: Buses run from the Terminal Norte to the site, about 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes, and cost a few dollars.
A tour from Mexico City includes transport and a guide, and often a stop at a shop or restaurant.
A taxi or Uber for the day is affordable in a group.
options.detail: Agree the price and waiting time.

gettingAround.intro: The site is large and walkable, with five entrances.

options.text: About 4–6 km round trip on flat paths. Very little shade.
options.detail: Wear a hat and comfortable shoes.

options.text: Taxis and tuk-tuks operate between gates.
A guide can plan an efficient route.

bestTime.headline: November–April
bestTime.summary: The site is exposed and hot. The dry winter months are best, and the rainy season brings afternoon storms.

seasons.text: Dry, sunny and cool in the morning.
Hot and dry. Go at opening. The spring equinox brings crowds.
Afternoon rain. Mornings are often clear.

bestTime.avoid: The spring equinox (around 21 March), when huge crowds gather, and Sundays, when the site is free for Mexicans and crowded.

itinerary.title: A day at Teotihuacán
itinerary.intro: The site at opening, lunch in a cave restaurant, and the museum. Assumes a bus or tour from Mexico City.

days.title: The City of the Gods
days.morning: The Avenue of the Dead and the pyramids of the Sun and Moon.
days.afternoon: Lunch, the Citadel and the museum.

tipsIntro: Teotihuacán is big and hot, and a few tips help.
tips: Go at opening, and take water, a hat and sunscreen.
Avoid Sundays and the spring equinox.
Book a licensed guide, or read up first.
Wear comfortable shoes, and expect steep steps.
Do not buy from unlicensed vendors pressing you on the paths.
Check whether climbing the pyramids is permitted.
Bring cash for entry, food and tips.

faq.q: How long do you need at Teotihuacán?
faq.a: Three to four hours for the main sights, and half a day with lunch and the museum.
Rules change. The Pyramid of the Sun has generally been open to climbing, while the Pyramid of the Moon has been closed. Check on arrival.
An unknown civilisation. The name is Aztec, and we do not know what its builders called themselves.

faq.q: How do I get there from Mexico City?
faq.a: By bus from the Terminal Norte (about an hour), a tour or a taxi.

faq.q: What is the best time of day to visit?
faq.a: Early morning, when it is cool and quiet.

faq.q: Can I combine it with other places?
faq.a: Yes. It combines with the Basilica of Guadalupe, and with Tepotzotlán or Puebla on the way onwards.
